items.title: GitHub Copilot assisted permissions generally available
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Assisted permissions are now generally available in GitHub Copilot CLI, GitHub Copilot app, and Visual Studio Code. When Copilot requests permission to run a command, access a file system path, or open a URL, a large language model evaluates the request. Requests classified as clearly safe automatically proceed. Other requests require your approval. GitHub Copilot CLI Run /permissions, then select assisted. GitHub Copilot app Open the mode picker, click Tool permissions, then select Assisted. Visual Studio Code Open the permissions picker, then select Assisted permissions. Enterprise controls If you’re an enterprise administrator, you can use enterprise-managed settings to block Allow All while keeping Assisted available or disable Assisted separately. You can also choose the default permission mode for new sessions. Developers can still select another mode permitted by policy. If the default is unavailable or prohibited by policy, the session starts with manual approval. For details about how assisted permissions evaluate requests and when approval is required, see Allowing safe commands to run without manual approval. The post GitHub Copilot assisted permissions generally available appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: Copilot now has LLM-assisted command and file permissions with enterprise controls. This is a useful reference for agent permission policies in Claude Code and Codex, and relevant for clients on Copilot.

items.title: GitHub Copilot supports server-to-server authentication
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: GitHub Copilot now supports server-to-server authentication for GitHub Apps installed on organizations, available in public preview. Services and agents built with the GitHub Copilot SDK can now make requests on behalf of an organization without relying on a signed-in user’s credentials. This workload-owned identity helps agents and automated services operate reliably at larger scale without tying their authentication or usage to individual users. Developers can give a GitHub App the read-only Copilot Requests organization permission, install the app on an organization, and pass a short-lived installation access token to the Copilot SDK. Usage is attributed and billed to the organization that owns the installation. The organization’s model policies, budgets, and spending controls apply. Organization owners can review which apps have access, identify app-attributed usage in AI usage CSV reports using the app_client_id field, and stop an app’s access by suspending or uninstalling it. To get started, see server-to-server authentication for the GitHub Copilot SDK and managing GitHub App access to your organization’s Copilot. The post GitHub Copilot supports server-to-server authentication appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: Copilot SDK agents can now authenticate as an org via GitHub Apps instead of user credentials, useful for clients building automated agent services on GitHub.

items.title: Coding From the Himalayas With an Offline AI Agent
items.author: Rittika Jindal
items.excerpt: When we talk about working remotely, we take a lot of things for granted, especially reliable internet and power. But sometimes, working remotely means trying to get something done on a flight, during a long train ride, or somewhere with little or no network. I moved to the foothills of the Himalayas a year ago. I love the peace of living here, but it also comes with its own challenges, including network and power outages. Things I didn’t think about as much before are now part of planning my work. I work as a Principal Engineer at Thomson Reuters, where I spend most of my time coding and reviewing my teammates’ code. Coding agents are already a big part of my everyday workflow, which made me curious about how much of that workflow I could keep using offline.Working from the foothills of the Himalayas. Photo of my workspace. If you’re someone like me, who enjoys working with technology but also finds peace in quiet, remote places where the network doesn’t always cooperate, this article is for you. It’s also for anyone who has wondered whether a coding agent can run entirely on their laptop, with the internet switched off. I tried running a coding agent locally on my laptop to see how much work I could actually get done offline. What can we do offline? A project already on your laptop gives us plenty to work with. We can ask an agent to explain an unfamiliar function, investigate a failing test, refactor a small piece of code, or help finish a feature. These tasks can run offline when the model, project dependencies and test tools are available locally. Downloading a new package or looking something up on the web will still need a connection. Where OpenCode fitsOpenCode is an open-source coding agent that works with your project. You give it a task, and it can read files, propose edits and run commands such as the test suite. items.title: How Anthropic ships Claude with Claude: Separating the Brain from the Hands
items.author: swyx .ai
items.excerpt: Watch the full episode on YouTube As we learned from the Anthropic S-1 filings yesterday, the lab has some of the highest revenue and research efficiency in human history, particularly with -126% loss to 19% GAAP profit turnaround in the last year. The company credits this to their two core loops: Improvement and Investment: Today we go inside how Anthropic works. Now the dust has settled on Opus 5.5 and it has lasted a month as the generally accepted #1 LLM in the world, we dive into its launch, and how Anthropic ships Claude with Claude with Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang, heads of Engineering and Product respectively. The team is working under two kinds of pressure. The models are getting more capable, which makes safe deployment and access decisions harder. At the same time, usage is growing fast enough that ordinary infrastructure choices—like how much CPU an API consumes—become strategic. Those problems meet in the product choices that reach developers. A model launch is also an API launch Anthropic's Opus 5.5 launch emphasizes both model quality and cost. We discuss feedback that the previous Opus generations were be too verbose, alongside the need for stronger intelligence per dollar. Anthropic says the new model costs less to run than its predecessor; the exact saving depends on the workload and its use of cached context. The less visible launch work involves changes to how people integrate the API. One example we discuss is protecting model reasoning against extraction used for distillation. Preserving thinking blocks across turns helps address this, but a new requirement can also break a customer's existing harness. Katelyn also describes what being part of early access programs actually looks like in practice: Customers run evaluations in their own harnesses, report surprising behavior, and sometimes pass along less formal impressions. The useful part is not just a benchmark score: it is seeing the model in environments and tasks Anthropic's own products
items.why_it_matters: Inside look at how Anthropic ships with Claude and its brain-versus-hands agent architecture, useful for agent design. The S-1 financial claims are context only.

items.title: GPT-6.1 Terra
items.excerpt: GPT-6.1 Terra It's always interesting to note which aspects of a new model are emphasized in the release announcement. In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, OpenAI went with visual reasoning and computer use: We’re introducing GPT-6.1 Terra, a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. A significant step up from GPT‑5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos. Terra sits in the same position as Sonnet in the Anthropic model collection - not the cheapest or the most expensive, making it harder to decide when to use it. Computer use is a good example of a task that benefits from a less expensive model, since you might put it to work on automated, repetitive tasks. OpenAI's Ted Sanders provided some useful advice in a comment on Hacker News: In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, I'd say Terra is probably better than Astra and Sol at technical communication, similar on vision and computer use (but much faster!), and a bit worse on most other things. For API developers, it's a nice midrange option if you want something cheaper than Sol but a lot smarter than Luna (especially for vision / computer use / communication). For subscribers, it's not a bombshell release - if you're hitting usage limits, maybe it helps you go a bit further, and if you want clearer communication or faster computer use, it can be a nice option to select. items.title: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox
items.excerpt: Research: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox webframe is a neat little project from Jeff Lindsay which lets you "run a web page like a program" - you point it at a URL or file and it executes it in a hidden headless web view and outputs console.log() to standard output and any exceptions to standard error. It's written in Go on top of the glaze library, which provides access to a system browser ("WKWebView on macOS, WebKitGTK on Linux, WebView2 on Windows") so it doesn't need to bundle its own browser engine. It reminds me of my own shot-scraper javascript tool, albeit in a much smaller package that doesn't depend on Playwright. I had Claude Opus 5.5 put it through its paces and prepare a research report for me. Here's the prompt I used: Explore https://github.com/tractordev/webframe try running it and put it though its paces, build a few exploratory prototypes, then evaluate it as a potential sandboxing tool and as a tool for scraping web pages using the same patterns encouraged by the "shot-scraper JavaScript" command (see simonw/shot-scraper on GitHub, docs directory) Tags: browsers, go, javascript, jeff-lindsay, shot-scraper
items.why_it_matters: Simon Willison evaluates webframe, a small Go tool that runs a web page headlessly from the CLI. It may be handy for scraping or sandbox experiments but is niche for client delivery.

items.title: How Anthropic ships the #1 LLM in the World — with Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang
items.author: Latent Space
items.excerpt: An agent’s sandbox can die without taking the whole agent with it. That’s the idea behind “the brain and the hands,” Anthropic’s architecture for Claude Managed Agents. Now that the dust has settled on Opus 5.5, it is universally agreed to be the best model in the world. In this conversation with Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang, Anthropic’s Heads of Engineering and of Product, goes inside the systems that turn model capabilities into products developers can use. We cover: - Why Anthropic separated the agent harness, session state and execution environment. - Letting agents use credentials without putting those credentials inside their sandboxes. - Rebuilding the Messages API from Python to Rust with Claude—and verifying the rewrite with shadow traffic. - Preventing model distillation while preserving the developer experience. - Memory, “dreaming,” agent evaluations and the work still left for human engineers. - How Anthropic’s own teams use Claude while keeping responsibility for their code and writing. The episode opens with swyx’s look at Anthropic’s S-1: revenue per employee, compute efficiency, and the improvement and investment loops behind the business. **Related links** - [Claude Opus 5.5](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-opus-5-5) — Performance, pricing and safeguards. - [The brain and the hands](https://www.anthropic.com/research/managed-agents) — The Managed Agents architecture. - [How Anthropic contains Claude](https://www.anthropic.com/research/how-we-contain-claude) — Isolation, credentials and network controls. - [Harnesses for long-running agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents) — Maintaining progress across context windows.
